H1("IV. Detailed Gap Analysis — Tail Coverage and Change of Control")
P("These are the two issues raised by Ms. Liu-Dorsey’s counsel. We address them first and in detail because, as you note, every incoming director will eventually be a former director relying on these protections.", align="j")

H2("Gap 1 — No Change-of-Control Tail Obligation; Policy Discovery Period Unavailable in a Transaction (Critical)")
P("**Agreement.** Section 11 contains a maintenance covenant (efforts-based; see Gap 2) and a post-service survival clause, but no obligation to purchase run-off or “tail” coverage upon a Change of Control. Section 17 requires a successor to assume the Agreement, but the assumed obligation is only the same efforts-based § 11 covenant. The Agreement’s own detailed “Change of Control” definition (§ 1(b)) is used only to shift the entitlement determination to Independent Counsel (§ 6(b)); it is not linked to insurance at all.", align="j")
P("**Policy.** The Policy has no change-in-control (transaction) clause — it neither converts automatically to run-off on an acquisition nor offers a pre-priced run-off option. The only extension mechanism is the Discovery Period in Section 10, which is structurally ill-suited to a transaction:", align="j")
B([
 "**Trigger limited to Insurer action.** The right arises only if the Policy “is not renewed by the Insurer” or is “cancelled by the Insurer for any reason other than non-payment” (§ 10.1; § 16.4). A Company-initiated non-renewal — the typical post-closing outcome when an acquiror folds the target into its own program — does not trigger it.",
 "**Barred by any replacement program.** No Discovery Period is available if the Named Insured “has obtained any replacement directors and officers liability insurance policy … from any insurer (including the Insurer)” (§ 10.4(a)). An acquiror that adds the target to its own D&O program (which may exclude pre-closing acts) arguably extinguishes the right.",
 "**Barred if the Company cancels.** No Discovery Period is available if the Policy “was cancelled at the request of the Named Insured” (§ 10.4(d); see § 16.3).",
 "**Controlled solely by the Company.** The election is “exercisable only by the Named Insured and is not transferable or assignable” (§ 10.1), and the Named Insured acts for all Insured Persons in making elections (§ 19). Post-closing, the Named Insured is controlled by the acquiror. Former directors have no independent right to elect or pay for it.",
 "**Short duration and short window.** Maximum 24 months at 175% of premium ($2,345,000); notice and payment must be received within 30 days after expiry (January 31, 2026 for the current term) (§§ 10.1–10.2).",
 "**No additional limits.** The Discovery Period shares the expiring aggregate limits (§ 10.5). Claims paid during the Policy Period reduce what is available to former directors during the tail.",
])
P("**Scenario.** Ferndale is acquired in 2027 in a cash merger. The acquiror cancels the Ferndale program at closing and adds Ferndale to its own D&O program, which excludes pre-closing Wrongful Acts. In 2029, stockholders sue the former Ferndale directors alleging a disclosure and process breach in the merger, or a securities claim regarding pre-closing clinical disclosures (the Exchange Act § 10(b) statute of repose is five years, 28 U.S.C. § 1658(b); Delaware fiduciary claims carry a three-year limitations period, 10 Del. C. § 8106, subject to tolling doctrines). The former directors have a contractual right to indemnification from the surviving corporation under § 17, but (i) there is no insurance behind it; (ii) the surviving corporation, now controlled by the acquiror, may resist indemnification and advancement, forcing enforcement litigation under § 9; and (iii) if the surviving entity is thinly capitalized or later becomes insolvent, there is no Side A. A merger-related stockholder claim is precisely the kind of claim most often brought after closing.", align="j")
P("**Who bears the risk.** Former directors, personally. The Company bears no cost until a transaction, which is why the provision is inexpensive to grant now.", align="j")
P("**Market practice.** In our experience, public-company merger agreements almost uniformly require the buyer to maintain the target’s D&O coverage for six years after closing, or permit the target to purchase a six-year prepaid tail before closing, subject to a cap on annual or aggregate premium expressed as a percentage of the target’s current annual premium (caps in the range of 200%–300% are typical). Because those protections depend on the target board negotiating them in the merger agreement, many public-company indemnification agreements now include a stand-alone contractual commitment so that directors are not dependent on the merger negotiation. Ms. Liu-Dorsey reports that both of her other public-company boards include such a provision, and Greystone has independently flagged the absence of one (Broker Summary §§ 5.5, 7.2). We recommend that Greystone provide current indicative six-year run-off pricing for the Committee’s file so that the cap can be validated against current life-sciences market conditions.", align="j")
P("**Recommendation — yes, amend the Agreement.** We recommend adding a new Section 11(d) with the following parameters: (i) trigger: consummation of any Change of Control as defined in § 1(b), and also any sale of all or substantially all assets or any dissolution; (ii) a prepaid, non-cancellable run-off for not less than six years after consummation, covering acts at or before closing (including the transaction itself); (iii) Side A and any excess Side A DIC coverage included; limits, retentions and terms no less favorable than those in effect immediately prior; (iv) aggregate premium cap of 300% of the last annual premium (approximately $4,020,000 at the current $1,340,000 premium), with a requirement to buy the best coverage available at the cap if full coverage costs more; (v) the obligation may be satisfied by an acquiror covenant in the merger agreement meeting the same standards, enforceable by the Indemnitee as a third-party beneficiary; (vi) no amendment or cancellation of the tail; (vii) binding on successors through § 17. Proposed language appears in Appendix B. We would also require Greystone to negotiate a change-in-control provision into the Policy at renewal (automatic conversion to run-off on a transaction with an option to purchase a six-year run-off at a pre-agreed premium), so that the contractual obligation can be satisfied efficiently with the incumbent carrier.", align="j")

H2("Gap 2 — Perpetual Indemnification versus Claims-Made Insurance; Efforts-Qualified Maintenance Covenant (High)")
P("**Agreement.** The indemnification and advancement obligations survive indefinitely and “shall not expire, lapse, or otherwise be limited by reason of the passage of time” (§ 17; see § 14), and are expressly primary and unaffected by whether insurance “is in force, has been cancelled, has expired, has been exhausted” (§ 12). By contrast, the insurance covenant is an efforts covenant (“commercially reasonable efforts”), qualified again by availability “on commercially reasonable terms” (§ 11(a), (c)). Upon termination, non-renewal or material reduction, the Company must only “promptly notify” the Indemnitee — after the fact — and use efforts to replace (§ 11(c)).", align="j")
P("**Policy.** Coverage is limited to Claims first made during the Policy Period or Discovery Period (Decl. Important Notice; §§ 1–3). Former directors are Insured Persons (“was, is, or shall hereafter become,” § 4.1), so a claim against a former director is covered by whatever policy is in force when the claim is made.", align="j")
P("**Analysis.** The concern in your email is valid but should be stated precisely. Claims-made coverage does not itself leave former directors uninsured: so long as the Company renews continuously and each renewal preserves the August 15, 2016 Continuity Date (prior-acts coverage), a former director sued years after departure is covered by the then-current policy. The gap arises when continuity breaks: (a) the Company elects not to renew or cannot obtain coverage on terms it regards as commercially reasonable (e.g., in financial distress, after a large loss, or in a hard market); (b) a replacement policy resets the continuity date or adds a prior-acts or specific-matter exclusion (§ 10.4(a) then also eliminates the Discovery Period); (c) a change of control (Gap 1); or (d) insolvency. In each case the Agreement leaves the director with a perpetual contractual right against a Company that is, by hypothesis, less able to pay. Because the covenant is efforts-qualified, the director would also have difficulty proving a breach.", align="j")
P("**Who bears the risk.** The Company directly (uninsured indemnity); former directors personally if the Company is insolvent or adverse.", align="j")
P("**Recommendation.** Amend § 11 to: (i) require that any renewal or replacement maintain at least the existing Side A limit and the existing Continuity Date (or full prior acts) and not add new prior-acts or specific-matter exclusions applicable to the Indemnitee without Board approval and notice; (ii) require 60 days’ advance written notice to directors (current and former) if the Company does not expect to bind renewal, and notice within 10 business days of receiving any Insurer non-renewal notice (the Insurer must give 90 days’ notice under Policy § 16.2); (iii) require the Company, if the program lapses without replacement, to purchase the longest available Discovery Period (currently 24 months) within the 30-day window and to use reasonable best efforts to obtain run-off of up to six years subject to the 300% cap; and (iv) give former directors the right, at their own cost if the Company declines, to require the Company to elect the Discovery Period on their behalf. At renewal, ask the Insurer to (x) make the Discovery Period available on any non-renewal (including by the Company), (y) extend the election window to 60 days, and (z) permit Insured Persons to elect it if the Named Insured does not.", align="j")

H1("V. Detailed Gap Analysis — Coverage Scope and Mechanics")

H2("Gap 3 — Insured-vs-Insured Exclusion: Company Claims, Bankruptcy Trustees and Derivative Participation (Critical)")
P("**Policy.** Section 5.2 excludes any Claim against an Insured Person brought “by, on behalf of, at the direction of, or with the active participation of the Company or any Insured Person,” including “through any receiver, trustee, assignee, or similar fiduciary acting on behalf of the Company.” The final paragraph confirms that the exclusion applies “without any carve-out” to “any Claim brought directly by the Company against a current or former director or officer,” including fiduciary-duty and clawback claims. Carve-backs are limited to (i) derivative actions “without the solicitation, assistance, active participation, or intervention of any current director or officer”; (ii) employment practices claims; (iii) whistleblower claims by former directors or officers absent 24 months; and (iv) cross-claims. There is no Side A carve-back and no carve-back for a bankruptcy trustee, examiner, creditors’ committee, liquidating or litigation trust, or for claims brought after a change of control.", align="j")
P("**Agreement.** Section 3 indemnifies only Expenses (not judgments or settlements) in proceedings “by or in the right of the Company,” and bars even Expenses if the Indemnitee is adjudged liable absent court approval, tracking DGCL § 145(b). Section 3’s final paragraph then states that direct claims by the Company “shall be governed by the provisions of Section 2” — i.e., the Company would indemnify judgments, fines and settlements in a suit the Company itself brings. In our view that sentence is unlikely to be enforceable as to judgments and settlements: § 145(a) by its terms applies to actions “other than an action by or in the right of the corporation,” a direct suit by the corporation is an action “by” the corporation, and Delaware courts have held that § 145(f) “non-exclusivity” cannot be used to grant indemnification inconsistent with the limits of § 145 (see, e.g., Waltuch v. Conticommodity Services, Inc., 88 F.3d 87 (2d Cir. 1996) (applying Delaware law)). Indemnifying a director against a judgment the Company itself obtains would also be circular. Expenses remain indemnifiable subject to § 145(b).", align="j")
P("**Analysis and scenarios.** The combination leaves directors exposed exactly when the Company becomes their adversary:", align="j")
B([
 "**Bankruptcy / litigation trust.** A clinical failure leads to a Chapter 11 filing. The plan creates a litigation trust that sues the former directors for breach of fiduciary duty (e.g., failure of oversight, cash burn). The trust sues “on behalf of the Company” as assignee/fiduciary — excluded by § 5.2(a), including under Side A. The Company (debtor) will not indemnify a claim it is prosecuting, and any indemnification claim is a prepetition unsecured claim. **Directors bear defense costs and any judgment personally.** This is among the most common sources of uninsured director loss in life-sciences insolvencies.",
 "**Post-change-of-control claims.** After an acquisition, the acquiror-controlled Company sues former directors (or brings clawback claims). Excluded entirely by the final paragraph of § 5.2. The Agreement’s § 17 successor assumption does not help, because the successor is the plaintiff.",
 "**Derivative participation trap.** A derivative suit is carved back only if no current director or officer has solicited, assisted, participated or intervened (§ 5.2(i); § 5.2(b) contains a similar condition for security-holder claims). A current director who cooperates with a plaintiff, a whistleblowing officer, or a special litigation committee that elects to take over or join the claim may forfeit coverage for all defendants. Derivative settlements and judgments are non-indemnifiable under § 145(b) and are therefore the core of Side A; this condition goes to the heart of what Side A is for.",
 "**Regulatory receivership.** Less relevant to Ferndale, but the receiver/conservator limb also applies.",
])
P("**Who bears the risk.** Directors personally. There is no Company layer in an adverse-Company claim.", align="j")
P("**Recommendation.** Negotiate an endorsement providing that the exclusion does not apply to: (a) any Claim brought by a bankruptcy trustee, examiner, receiver, liquidator, creditors’ committee, assignee for the benefit of creditors, or liquidating or litigation trust (or any assignee of such persons); (b) any Claim brought after a change in control by or on behalf of the Company or its successor; (c) any Claim brought by the Company in a foreign jurisdiction where suit by the Company is required; (d) any Loss under Side A, whatever the claimant; and (e) derivative claims unless an Insured Person actively solicited the claim (mere cooperation as a witness, whistleblower activity, or SLC process should not trigger the exclusion). These are commonly available in the current market. The Excess Side A DIC policy recommended below should contain these carve-backs as a matter of course. In the Agreement, revise the last paragraph of § 3 to state that the Company will indemnify direct-claim Expenses and, to the extent judgments or settlements are not indemnifiable, will cooperate in making insurance available and will not oppose a § 145(b) court application.", align="j")

H2("Gap 4 — Life-Sciences Exclusions Applicable to Side A Without Carve-Backs (Critical)")
P("**Policy.** Three exclusions are drafted broadly and apply to all Insuring Clauses:", align="j")
B([
 "**Bodily Injury / Property Damage (§ 5.3):** any Claim “for, based upon, or alleging” bodily injury, sickness, disease, emotional distress, or death.",
 "**Professional Services (§ 5.7):** any Claim “alleging, arising out of, based upon, or attributable to the rendering of or failure to render professional services … including but not limited to the provision of scientific, medical, pharmaceutical, clinical, consulting, advisory, research, or laboratory services.”",
 "**Pollution (§ 5.5):** “Pollutants” includes “pharmaceutical waste, biohazardous materials, genetically modified organisms.”",
])
P("None contains the carve-backs that are customary in public-company D&O forms: for Securities Claims, for derivative claims, and for Side A (non-indemnifiable) Loss. The ERISA exclusion (§ 5.4) shows the drafter knew how to write a Side A carve-back; it was not given here.", align="j")
P("**Agreement.** Section 7 is the “sole and exclusive” list of exclusions; it contains no BI/PD, professional services or pollution exclusion. The Company therefore must indemnify these claims in full.", align="j")
P("**Why this matters for Ferndale.** The Company’s core business is clinical development; the 2021 derivative suit alleged fiduciary breaches “in connection with the Company’s clinical trial disclosures” (Broker Summary § 6.1). The typical life-sciences securities class action and follow-on derivative suit alleges that management and the board misrepresented clinical trial results or safety signals — an allegation that, under § 5.7’s “arising out of … clinical … research” language and § 5.3’s “alleging … bodily injury” language, an insurer could argue is excluded in whole or in part. A stock-drop suit following a patient death in a trial is the paradigm case.", align="j")
P("**Scenario.** A Phase 3 trial is halted after serious adverse events. Securities and derivative suits follow, alleging the board ignored safety signals. The Insurer reserves rights under §§ 5.3 and 5.7. While the Company is solvent it must advance and indemnify under the Agreement with no assurance of Side B or Side C reimbursement (an uninsured exposure easily in the eight figures for a $2.8 billion company). If the trial failure precipitates insolvency, Side A is subject to the same exclusions — the directors’ personal backstop fails at the moment it is needed.", align="j")
P("**Recommendation.** Endorse each of §§ 5.3, 5.5 and 5.7 to (i) carve back Securities Claims and derivative claims, (ii) carve back all Loss under Insuring Clause A, and (iii) change “arising out of … in any way involving” to “for” (actual bodily injury or professional-services damages claims). Confirm that the Company carries products liability / clinical trials liability insurance and that the D&O “other insurance” exclusion (§ 5.6) cannot be read to exclude D&O claims merely because a clinical-trial policy exists. A properly drafted Excess Side A DIC policy should not contain these exclusions.", align="j")

H2("Gap 5 — Trigger Mismatch: “Proceeding” versus “Claim”; Pre-Claim Costs; Witness Costs (High)")
P("**Agreement.** “Proceeding” includes any “threatened, pending, or completed” action and any “investigation (whether formal or informal), inquiry, hearing, or any other actual or threatened proceeding” (§ 1(i)). The Company must indemnify Expenses as a witness or for responding to subpoenas or discovery without any standard-of-conduct determination (§ 4), and must advance all Expenses within 30 days (§ 5). “Expenses” include costs of “preparing to … defend, investigating, being or preparing to be a witness” (§ 1(f)).", align="j")
P("**Policy.** “Claim” (§ 4.2) requires a written demand, a commenced proceeding, or a “formal” investigation commenced by an order or notice that “specifically identifies the Insured Person by name,” or a subpoena, target letter or Wells notice. It expressly excludes informal inquiries that do not identify the Insured Person “as a target, subject, or person of interest” (§ 4.2(ii)); preliminary investigations without a formal order (§ 4.2(iii)); mere requests for information, documents or testimony (§ 4.2(v)); and threatened actions (§ 4.2(vi)). Defense Costs exclude “any amount incurred prior to the date the Claim is first made” (§ 4.5(iii)). Notice of circumstances (§ 6.4) locks in coverage for a later Claim but does not make pre-Claim costs recoverable.", align="j")
P("**The 2023 SEC inquiry under the current wording.** The SEC’s inquiry was initiated by “a voluntary document request letter directed to the Company” and did not name individuals (Broker Summary § 6.2). Under the current § 4.2 it is not a Claim against any Insured Person (it falls squarely within exclusions (ii), (iii) and (v)), and the Company-entity costs (including Pinnacle Forensic Accounting) are not insured at all because Side C covers only Securities Claims against the Company. Even had it been a Claim, Side B would apply only above the $1,000,000 per-Claim retention, so at most roughly $100,000 of the $1,100,000 spent would have been recoverable. The $850,000 negotiated recovery under the prior policy is therefore not a reliable precedent; the current definition appears, if anything, to codify the Insurer’s 2023 position. (The Broker Summary states that the renewal added no restrictions; we recommend obtaining the prior-year form to confirm whether § 4.2 was narrowed.)", align="j")
P("**Scenario for an incoming director.** Mr. Kjelland, a former Fortune 500 CFO, is likely to chair or sit on the Audit Committee. The SEC’s Division of Enforcement opens an informal inquiry into revenue recognition and requests a voluntary interview with Audit Committee members. Mr. Kjelland retains personal counsel. Under the Agreement (§§ 4, 5) the Company must advance his fees; none of those fees is insured until (and unless) he receives a subpoena, Wells notice or is named in a formal order. If the Company is in distress, his personal counsel fees are unprotected.", align="j")
P("**Who bears the risk.** The Company, as an uninsured advancement and witness-cost obligation; directors only if the Company cannot or will not pay.", align="j")
P("**Recommendation.** At renewal (or mid-term if available) obtain: (i) an expanded Claim definition including any written request to an Insured Person to appear for an interview or meeting, or to produce documents, by an enforcement authority (SEC, DOJ, FDA, state AG, foreign regulator), and civil investigative demands; (ii) “pre-claim inquiry” coverage for Insured Persons’ costs of responding to informal or entity-level inquiries, with no retention; (iii) an entity investigation costs sublimit (to address costs such as Pinnacle’s); and (iv) derivative demand investigation costs coverage for the Board’s evaluation of stockholder demands. Greystone has already suggested items (ii)–(iii) (Broker Summary § 7.1).", align="j")

H2("Gap 6 — Scope of “Loss”: Fines, Penalties, Taxes, Compliance Costs, Disgorgement and Restitution (High)")
P("**Agreement.** Indemnifiable amounts include “Fines” — “any fine, penalty, or excise tax,” including ERISA excise taxes (§ 1(g)); the Company expressly “acknowledges” that § 2 extends to “Fines and penalties imposed by any governmental authority” (§ 2); “Expenses” include taxes on indemnification payments (gross-up) and “the costs of complying with any court order, consent decree, judgment, or other directive” (§ 1(f)); and “Amounts Paid in Settlement” include the value of non-monetary consideration (§ 1(j)).", align="j")
P("**Policy.** “Loss” excludes fines and penalties except where insurable under the most favorable law “as determined by the Insurer in its reasonable discretion” (§ 4.4 (i)); taxes (ii); compensation (iv); uninsurable matters (v); and the costs of compliance with injunctive or non-monetary relief, “disgorgement of profits, restitution, or other corrective actions” (vi). Punitive damages are covered only “where insurable under applicable law” without a most-favorable-jurisdiction rule (§ 4.4 (i) of the inclusions). The Insurer may withhold consent to settlements imposing non-monetary obligations (§ 7.2(b)).", align="j")
P("**Analysis.** Each of these is a Company-funded, uninsured obligation. Two deserve particular attention. First, the restitution/disgorgement language could be invoked against settlements of Securities Act §§ 11 and 12 claims (which insurers have characterized as restitutionary); Ferndale’s offering activity makes this a live issue, and a §§ 11/12 carve-back is customary. Second, the insurer-discretion qualifier on fines undermines an otherwise favorable most-favorable-law clause. We note that the Delaware Supreme Court has held that Delaware law governs the insurability analysis for D&O policies of Delaware corporations and that Delaware public policy does not bar coverage of fraud-based loss (RSUI Indemnity Co. v. Murdock, 248 A.3d 887 (Del. 2021)); the Policy’s Delaware choice of law (§ 20) is helpful in that respect. Separately, the SEC takes the position that indemnification of Securities Act liabilities is against public policy (Regulation S-K Item 512(h) undertaking) and typically requires that civil penalties not be indemnified or insured, so insurance cannot fully close the penalties gap.", align="j")
P("**Who bears the risk.** The Company; directors if the Company is insolvent (Side A has the same definition of Loss).", align="j")
P("**Recommendation.** Endorse “Loss” to (i) delete “as determined by the Insurer in its reasonable discretion”; (ii) apply most-favorable-jurisdiction wording to punitive, exemplary and multiplied damages; (iii) add a carve-back providing that Loss includes amounts payable for violations of Sections 11, 12 and 15 of the Securities Act notwithstanding the restitution/disgorgement exclusion; and (iv) cover civil penalties under FCPA § 78dd-2(g)(2)(B) and similar provisions where insurable. No change to the Agreement is required; the Committee should simply understand that fines and compliance costs will generally be uninsured.", align="j")

H2("Gap 7 — Limits, Retention and Erosion (High)")
P("**Policy.** $25,000,000 Side A dedicated; $25,000,000 Side B/C combined; defense costs erode all limits; $1,000,000 retention per Claim for Sides B and C; all limits are aggregates for the Policy Period and any Discovery Period (Decl. Items 4–5; §§ 1–3, 10.5). Related claims are a single Claim, deemed made on the earliest date (§§ 4.2, 4.7).", align="j")
P("**Agreement.** Unlimited in amount; primary (§ 12).", align="j")
P("**Analysis.** (i) **Side B/C sharing.** A single securities class action naming the Company and its directors consumes the shared $25M for both the entity (Side C) and the individuals (Side B). Entity defense and settlement can exhaust the tower, after which all further indemnification of directors is uninsured Company cost. Side A does not “drop down” merely because Side B is exhausted: so long as the Company is able and willing to indemnify, the Loss is indemnifiable and outside Side A. (ii) **Side A sharing.** The $25M Side A limit is shared among all past, present and future directors and officers for all Claims in the year — nine directors plus the officer group. In a large derivative settlement (the classic Side A loss), the limit may be consumed by settlement contributions and defense costs of management defendants, leaving little for independent directors. (iii) **Retention.** The $1M per-Claim retention is borne by the Company; because Endorsement No. 2 treats refusal or inability to indemnify as Non-Indemnifiable Loss, and Side A has no retention, a director is not personally exposed for the retention — a meaningful strength. (iv) **Tail limits.** A Discovery Period adds no limits (§ 10.5). (v) **Adequacy.** Greystone describes the limits as typical for the Company’s size (Broker Summary § 7.3) but itself suggests evaluating excess Side A or Side A DIC capacity.", align="j")
P("**Who bears the risk.** The Company first; independent directors personally in a high-severity or multi-claim year or upon insolvency.", align="j")
P("**Recommendation.** Purchase an Excess Side A DIC policy (we suggest pricing $15M–$25M) with: broad DIC drop-down over the underlying exclusions and when the underlying insurer fails or refuses to pay; no Insured-vs-Insured exclusion for bankruptcy trustees and post-change-of-control claims; no BI/PD, professional services or pollution exclusion except for direct bodily-injury claims; and a non-rescindable form. Evaluate a dedicated Independent Director Liability (IDL) policy for the non-management directors, which directly answers the candidates’ concern that they share Side A limits with management. Ask Greystone for a limits-adequacy benchmark against life-sciences peers, including settlement-severity data.", align="j")

P("**Recommendation.** Seek a 30-day advancement endorsement; an allocation endorsement providing 100% coverage of Defense Costs of Insured Persons for covered Claims (with relative-exposure allocation reserved for settlements and judgments); and a pre-approved panel or rate schedule (including Caldwell Morton & Sage LLP, which defended the 2021 action) so that counsel consent is not an issue at the outset of a matter.", align="j")

H2("Gap 9 — Settlement Consent and the Hammer Clause (Medium–High)")
P("**Agreement.** The Company need not indemnify settlements made without its consent, which may not be unreasonably withheld, and is deemed given after 30 days’ silence (§ 7(d)).", align="j")
P("**Policy.** The Insurer’s consent is required for any settlement and may be withheld if the settlement lacks a full release of all Insured Persons, imposes non-monetary obligations, involves an admission, or is funded from non-Loss sources (§ 7.2). Insureds may not admit liability or incur expense without consent (§ 7.4). A full hammer clause caps the Insurer’s liability at the recommended settlement plus Defense Costs to date if “the Named Insured or the Insured Person” refuses an Insurer-recommended settlement, with all later Loss “borne solely by the Named Insured or the Insured Person” (§ 7.3).", align="j")
P("**Scenarios.** (a) The Company consents to (or is deemed under § 7(d) to consent to) a settlement the Insurer has not approved — the Company has indemnification liability with no Side B reimbursement. The severability provisions (§ 11.1 and Endorsement No. 1, §§ 11.3–11.4) apply only to the Conduct Exclusion and to the Application; § 5.8(b) therefore is imputed across all Insured Persons. Interrelated Claims are deemed first made at the earliest date, and if earlier than inception, are not covered (§ 4.7).", align="j")
P("**Agreement.** Knowledge of any other director or officer is not imputed to the Indemnitee for indemnification purposes (§ 8).", align="j")
P("**Analysis.** (i) Clause (a) operates as a prior-acts exclusion for pre-2016 conduct; it is unlikely to affect the incoming directors directly but remains a Company exposure. H2("Gap 11 — Conduct Exclusion Adjudication Venue and Lead-In (Medium)")

 ["Insurer-recommended settlement refused", "Company indemnifies excess (uninsured)", "Director bears post-recommendation loss", "**Medium**", "Soft hammer"],
 ["Claim after director rotates off, program renewed continuously", "Indemnified; covered by then-current policy", "Side A under then-current policy", "Low", "§ 11 continuity covenant"],
 ["Claim after program lapses (no renewal)", "Indemnified; uninsured after 24-month maximum Discovery Period", "No insurance", "**High**", "§ 11(e) lapse covenant"],
], widths=[1.55, 1.35, 1.35, 1.0, 1.25], size=8)

B([

 "**Margaret Liu-Dorsey (governance academic; two other public boards).** Her counsel’s focus on tail coverage is well-founded (Gaps 1–2). Because she sits on other boards, Side A’s primacy (§ 13.2) is helpful; she should confirm that her other companies’ programs do not purport to be excess of Ferndale’s. We recommend granting her requested tail provision (Appendix B).",
])
P("**Common to all three.** Each will be a new director with no knowledge of historical matters; non-imputation under the Agreement (§ 8) and Policy (§ 11) is a genuine strength, but § 5.8(b) prior-knowledge imputation (Gap 10) is an exception that should be fixed.  ["A-2", "New § 11(d): mandatory six-year prepaid change-of-control tail; terms no less favorable; includes Side A / DIC; 300% aggregate premium cap with best-available fallback; may be satisfied by acquiror covenant with third-party-beneficiary rights; non-cancellable; binding on successors (Appendix B).", "Gap 1", "Immediate"],
 ["A-3", "New § 11(e): on lapse without replacement, purchase longest available Discovery Period within the election window and pursue up to six-year run-off within the cap; former directors may require the election.", "Gap 2", "Immediate"],

 ["A-5", "New insolvency cooperation covenant (Side A proceeds not estate property; stay-relief cooperation).", "Gap 13", "Immediate"],
 ["A-6", "Revise § 10 second paragraph to eliminate any implied Indemnitee contribution obligation.", "Gap 15", "Immediate"],
 ["A-7", "Carve out Side A / DIC recoveries from the § 13 consent requirement where the Company has failed to indemnify, is insolvent or is adverse.", "Gap 15", "Immediate"],
 ["A-8", "Revise § 7(d): no withholding of consent solely for lack of insurer consent; no Company consent on the director’s behalf to settlements lacking a full release or imposing admissions/non-monetary terms.", "Gap 9", "Immediate"],
 ["A-9", "Revise § 3 final paragraph (direct Company claims) to reflect § 145(b) limits and add cooperation/no-opposition to court applications and Side A access.", "Gap 3", "Immediate"],
 ["A-10", "Extend “Corporate Status” to director-nominee status; confirm Indemnitee may notify insurers directly.", "Gaps 14, 15", "Immediate"],

 ["B-3", "Insured-vs-Insured carve-backs: bankruptcy trustee/committee/litigation trust; post-change-in-control; all Side A Loss; narrow derivative-participation condition; whistleblower carve-back for any Insured Person.", "Gap 3", "Now / renewal"],

 ["B-9", "Extend severability to § 5.8(b); limit Conduct-Exclusion adjudication to the underlying action.", "Gaps 10–11", "Renewal"],

], widths=[0.45, 4.0, 0.9, 1.15], size=8)
H2("C. Supplemental Insurance")
B([

 ["2021 derivative suit (C.A. No. 2021-0473-SG, Del. ], widths=[1.2, 1.6, 2.2, 1.5], size=8)
P("We also note internal inconsistencies in the claims history that should be reconciled before it is shared with candidates: the derivative case caption appears as “Fenwick” in your email and “Ferndale” in the Broker Summary; and the $850,000 SEC recovery is difficult to reconcile with a $1,000,000 Side B retention, suggesting either a different prior-year retention or a negotiated compromise outside the policy terms.", align="j")
H2("B. Open Items and Information Requests")
N([
 "Exact legal name of the Company and any former names; whether “Fenwick BioSciences, Inc.” is a former name or a separate entity.",
 "Correct identity of the issuing insurer (Ridgemont / Oakvale) and a re-executed Policy.",
 "Certificate of Incorporation and Bylaws (indemnification and § 102(b)(7) provisions; whether officer exculpation under amended § 102(b)(7) has been adopted).",
 "Prior-year D&O policies (to compare the “Claim” definition), loss runs and notices for the 2021 and 2023 matters; remaining prior-year limits.",
 "The 2021 derivative settlement stipulation and allocation of the $3.2M.",
 "Any excess D&O layers, fiduciary, EPL, clinical trials/products and cyber policies.",
 "The policy Application and any warranty letters (relevant to severability and rescission).",
 "Greystone indicative pricing: Excess Side A DIC, IDL, six-year run-off, and the B-2 through B-10 endorsements.",
])
P("This memorandum is based on the documents identified in Section II and on Delaware law as we understand it as of the date above; it does not address the law of other jurisdictions. Market-practice observations reflect our experience and should be confirmed with current broker data. We would be pleased to prepare the amended form Agreement and the candidate-facing summary on the Committee’s instruction. A budget estimate for this engagement is being provided under separate cover.", italic=True, align="j", size=10)
EOF

**PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL**

**ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION --- ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT**

*Prepared by outside counsel at the request of the General Counsel for the purpose of rendering legal advice to Ferndale BioSciences, Inc. and its Board of Directors (Nominating and Governance Committee). Do not forward outside the Committee without consulting counsel.*

**HARCOURT NASH LLP**

225 Franklin Street, 22nd Floor, Boston, MA 02110

**MEMORANDUM**

  --------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  TO:       Helena Marchetti, General Counsel & Corporate Secretary, Ferndale BioSciences, Inc. (for distribution to the Nominating and Governance Committee of the Board of Directors, under privilege)

  FROM:     Nathaniel Reeves, Harcourt Nash LLP

  DATE:     April 25, 2025

  RE:       Coverage Gap Analysis --- Oakvale Specialty D&O Policy No. RSI-DO-2025-07741 (Policy Period January 1, 2025 -- January 1, 2026) versus Form Indemnification Agreement (Form Approved March 15, 2025); Implications for Incoming Independent Directors Dr. Priya Ramaswamy, Thomas Kjelland and Margaret Liu-Dorsey
  --------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# I. Executive Summary

You asked us to compare the Company's 2025 D&O liability insurance policy (the "Policy") against the form director and officer Indemnification Agreement (the "Agreement") that will be presented to the three incoming independent directors, to identify every material gap, overlap and inconsistency, to assess real-world impact from the perspective of the incoming directors, to recommend fixes, and to identify where the protections are strong. We reviewed the Policy (Declarations, General Terms and Conditions Sections 1--20, and Endorsements RSI-DO-END-001 through -003), the Agreement (Sections 1--18), the Greystone Brokerage Partners Coverage Summary and Placement Memorandum dated April 2, 2025 (the "Broker Summary"), and your engagement email of April 7, 2025.

**Bottom line.** The Agreement is a strong, indemnitee-favorable document that tracks DGCL § 145 and current Delaware practice. The Policy has a well-constructed Side A core (dedicated, non-eroding \$25 million limit; no retention; primary; first priority of payment; express response when the Company refuses or is unable to indemnify; final-adjudication conduct exclusion; strong application severability). The two instruments, however, were not drafted to fit each other, and the misfit is greatest in exactly the situations in which an independent director most needs protection: when the Company cannot or will not pay (insolvency, change of control, a hostile post-transaction or post-bankruptcy board, a trustee or litigation trust) and when the Company's obligations are triggered earlier or more broadly than the Policy responds. In those situations the Agreement promises far more than the Policy funds, and the difference falls first on the Company's balance sheet and, if the Company is unable or unwilling to pay, on the directors personally.

**Most significant gaps (ranked).**

  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **\#**   **Gap**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          **Severity**          **Who bears it**                                                           **Primary fix**
  -------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- --------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1        No change-of-control tail obligation in the Agreement; the Policy's Discovery Period is in practice unavailable in an M&A transaction (available only on Insurer non-renewal/cancellation; barred if any replacement policy is bought or if the Company cancels; Named-Insured-only; 24-month maximum; no added limits) (Agreement § 11; Policy §§ 10.1, 10.4(a), 10.4(d), 10.5, 16.3, 19).                                                                      Critical              Former directors (personally) once the acquiror controls the Company       New Agreement § 11(d) mandatory 6-year prepaid tail (300% premium cap) + negotiated change-in-control run-off endorsement

  2        Insured-vs-Insured exclusion bars all claims by the Company, and claims brought through a receiver, trustee or assignee, with no Side A or bankruptcy carve-back; derivative carve-back is conditioned on no participation by any current director or officer (Policy § 5.2). Agreement § 3 purports to indemnify judgments/settlements in direct Company claims, which § 145(b) likely does not permit.                                                         Critical              Directors personally (Company is the adverse party)                        Endorsement: bankruptcy-trustee, creditor-committee, litigation-trust and post-change-of-control carve-backs; Side A carve-back for all Company claims; narrow participation condition

  3        Biotech-critical exclusions --- Bodily Injury (§ 5.3), Professional Services incl. "clinical ... research ... laboratory services" (§ 5.7) and Pollution incl. "pharmaceutical waste, biohazardous materials" (§ 5.5) --- apply to every Insuring Clause, including Side A, with "arising out of ... in any way involving" wording and no securities-claim or derivative carve-back. The Agreement (§ 7, exclusive list) contains no corresponding exclusions.   Critical              Company (uninsured indemnity); directors personally if Company insolvent   Carve-backs for Securities Claims, derivative claims and all Side A Loss; Excess Side A DIC

  4        Trigger mismatch: Agreement "Proceeding" covers threatened, informal and witness matters; Policy "Claim" excludes informal inquiries, voluntary document requests and pre-targeting investigations, and Defense Costs exclude pre-Claim costs (Policy §§ 4.2, 4.5(iii); Agreement §§ 1(i), 4, 5). The 2023 SEC inquiry would likely receive no reimbursement under the current wording.                                                                          High                  Company (uninsured advancement)                                            Pre-claim inquiry / informal investigation coverage for Insured Persons; entity investigation sublimit

  5        Loss excludes fines, penalties, taxes, compliance costs, disgorgement and restitution (Policy § 4.4) that the Agreement expressly indemnifies (Agreement §§ 1(f), 1(g), 2).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      High                  Company; directors if Company cannot pay                                   Most-favorable-jurisdiction wording without insurer discretion; Securities Act §§ 11/12 carve-back

  6        Limits, retention and erosion: \$1M per-Claim Side B/C retention; \$25M B/C shared and eroded by entity securities defense; single \$25M Side A shared by every director and officer across all Claims; no excess or DIC layer; Discovery Period adds no limits.                                                                                                                                                                                                 High                  Company first; directors in a large or multi-claim year                    Excess Side A DIC (and consider a dedicated Independent Director Liability policy)

  7        Advancement mechanics misaligned: Agreement 30 days / counsel of Indemnitee's choice vs. Policy 60 days / Insurer consent to counsel / 70% interim allocation (Agreement § 5; Policy §§ 7.1, 8.3, 9.3).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          Medium--High          Company (float); directors in Side A scenario                              30-day advancement; 100% interim advancement for Insured Persons; pre-approved counsel

  8        Full "hammer" clause; insurer settlement-consent grounds broader than the Agreement's consent standard (Policy §§ 7.2--7.4; Agreement § 7(d)).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   Medium--High          Company; director personally in Side A scenario                            Soft hammer (80/20), no hammer for Side A

  9        Prior-knowledge and prior-notice exclusion is not severable (one person's knowledge excludes everyone) and sweeps in matters noticed under prior policies (Policy §§ 5.8, 11.1; End. No. 1).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     Medium--High          All Insured Persons                                                        Extend severability to § 5.8; confirm prior-policy limits

  10       Document-integrity defects: the Agreement names "Fenwick BioSciences, Inc." while the Policy insures "Ferndale BioSciences, Inc."; the Policy is headed and signed by "Ridgemont Specialty Insurance Co." but issued (per its body, Declarations Item 9 and the Broker Summary) by "Oakvale Specialty Insurance Co."; the Broker Summary misstates several terms.                                                                                                High (easily fixed)   Everyone --- risks a coverage dispute at the outset of any Claim           Corrective endorsement; conform Agreement; correct Broker Summary
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Where the protections are strong.** The Committee can tell the candidates with confidence that: (i) the Agreement provides mandatory, unconditional advancement within 30 days on an unsecured undertaking, a presumption of entitlement with a clear-and-convincing burden on the Company, deemed approval after 60 days, fee-shifting for enforcement, independent-counsel determinations after a change of control, successor assumption, and survival without time limit; (ii) the Policy's Side A is dedicated (\$25 million, not eroded by Side B or C), carries no retention, is primary to other insurance, is paid first, and responds when the Company refuses or is financially unable to indemnify (Endorsement No. 2); (iii) the conduct exclusion requires a final, non-appealable adjudication and defense costs are advanced until then; (iv) application misstatements are imputed only to the CEO and CFO; (v) the Policy is non-cancellable by the Insurer except for non-payment; and (vi) both instruments are governed by Delaware law. Section VI catalogs these strengths.

**Key recommendations.** (1) Amend the Agreement before the incoming directors sign it --- most importantly to add a mandatory six-year change-of-control tail with a 300% premium cap, a lapse-without-replacement Discovery Period obligation, an insolvency cooperation covenant, the correct corporate name, and clean-up of Sections 10 and 13. (2) Obtain a corrective endorsement now on insurer identity and named insured, and negotiate mid-term (or no later than the January 1, 2026 renewal) endorsements addressing the Insured-vs-Insured, biotech exclusion, Claim/pre-claim, Loss, advancement, hammer, severability and run-off issues. (3) Purchase an excess Side A DIC layer (and evaluate a dedicated Independent Director Liability policy) so that the three incoming independent directors are not relying solely on a \$25 million Side A limit shared with management. We recommend that Liu-Dorsey's request for an explicit tail provision be granted; it is consistent with market practice and costs the Company nothing unless and until a transaction occurs. Section VIII sets out an action plan with timing.

**Privilege note.** The candidates and their personal counsel are not yet directors and are third parties to the Company's privilege. Sharing this memorandum with them risks waiver. We recommend preparing a separate, non-privileged summary of protections (and of agreed enhancements) for delivery to the candidates.
